description: Why electrolysis works, electrode reactions, electrolysis of brine, and aluminium extraction.
content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to decompose an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte, and it must be either molten or dissolved in water so that the ions are free to move and carry charge.

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes: the cathode (negative electrode) and the anode (positive electrode). Positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode; negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode. A useful mnemonic is PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Key Fact

At the cathode (negative): positive ions gain electrons — this is reduction. At the anode (positive): negative ions lose electrons — this is oxidation. Remember: electrolysis involves both oxidation and reduction simultaneously.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

When a molten ionic compound is electrolysed, only the ions of that compound are present. The metal ion moves to the cathode and is deposited as the metal; the non-metal ion moves to the anode and is released as the non-metal element. For example, molten lead bromide produces lead metal at the cathode and bromine gas at the anode. The key requirement is that the compound is molten — solid ionic compounds cannot conduct electricity because the ions are held in a fixed lattice and are not free to move. Dissolving the compound in water also frees the ions, though this introduces additional complexity because water provides its own ions.

It is important to understand that the electrolyte is not simply “broken down” into smaller pieces — it is chemically decomposed into its constituent elements. This makes electrolysis a powerful tool for extracting reactive metals that cannot be produced by simpler reduction methods. The external electrical supply acts as an electron pump: the power supply removes electrons from the anode (making it positive) and pushes electrons into the cathode (making it negative). Ions in the electrolyte carry charge through the solution between the electrodes, completing the circuit.

For molten lead bromide electrolysis:

Cathode (reduction): \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\)

Anode (oxidation): \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\)

Half-equations must be balanced for both atoms and charge. At the cathode, electrons are gained (shown on the left side of the arrow). At the anode, electrons are released (shown on the right side). The number of electrons must cancel when the two half-equations are combined.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the solution also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water itself. This means there is competition at each electrode between different ions. The rules for predicting products are:

  • Cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced from \(H^+\) ions. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.
  • Anode: If a halide ion (Cl²³, Br²³, I²³) is present in large amounts, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions).

Brine is concentrated sodium chloride solution. During electrolysis of brine, three useful products are obtained:

  • Cathode: hydrogen gas is produced (sodium is too reactive to be deposited; \(H^+\) ions are discharged instead).
  • Anode: chlorine gas is produced (chloride ions are present in high concentration and are preferentially discharged).
  • Remaining solution: sodium hydroxide (NaOH) remains in solution, as the sodium and hydroxide ions are not discharged.

The three products — hydrogen, chlorine, and sodium hydroxide — are all industrially important: chlorine is used to make bleach and PVC; hydrogen is used as a fuel; sodium hydroxide is used to make soap and paper.

Extraction of Aluminium

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon. Instead, it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)). The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and reduce energy costs.

Key Fact

Aluminium is deposited at the cathode (\(Al^{3+}\) ions gain electrons). Oxygen is released at the anode (\(O^{2-}\) ions lose electrons). The carbon anodes gradually burn away because the oxygen produced reacts with them at high temperature, so they need regular replacement. The process uses large amounts of electricity, making aluminium expensive to produce.

Practical Electrolysis (PAG C2)

In your practical work (PAG C2), you will investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert (carbon) electrodes. A typical investigation uses copper sulfate solution or brine. To test the gases produced: hold a lit splint near the cathode to detect hydrogen (squeaky pop); hold damp litmus paper near the anode to detect chlorine (paper bleaches) or use a glowing splint to detect oxygen (relights). Record which gas appears at which electrode and compare your results with predictions from competition rules.

Electroplating is another important application of electrolysis. To electroplate an object with copper: make the object the cathode, use a copper electrode as the anode, and use copper sulfate solution as the electrolyte. Copper atoms at the anode dissolve into solution as copper ions; the same mass of copper deposits on the cathode. The object gains a thin, evenly spread copper layer. Electroplating is used in jewellery (silver plating), corrosion protection (zinc plating on steel, called galvanising) and in electronics (copper tracks on circuit boards).

Higher Tier half-equations for aluminium extraction:

Cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\)

Anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\)
exam_tip_html: In questions on electrolysis of aqueous solutions, always check whether the metal is more or less reactive than hydrogen — this determines whether you get hydrogen gas or the metal at the cathode. At the anode, halide ions take priority over hydroxide ions (so chlorine is produced from brine, not oxygen). A very common error is stating that sodium is produced at the cathode during electrolysis of brine — sodium is too reactive, so hydrogen is produced instead. Higher Tier: when writing half-equations, always balance atoms first, then balance charge using electrons. State clearly which electrode each half-equation applies to.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis uses electricity to decompose ionic compounds. The electrolyte must be molten or dissolved. Positive ions move to the cathode (reduction — gain electrons); negative ions move to the anode (oxidation — lose electrons). PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
  • In aqueous solutions, competition occurs between ions. Cathode: hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; metal is deposited if less reactive. Anode: halide ions → halogen produced; no halide → oxygen produced. Electrolysis of brine gives hydrogen (cathode), chlorine (anode), and sodium hydroxide (remaining solution).
  • Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite (to lower the melting point). Aluminium forms at the cathode; oxygen at the anode. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing. The process is energy-intensive and therefore expensive.

practice_questions.text:
During electrolysis, which electrode do positive ions (cations) move towards?
A) The anode
B) The cathode
C) Both electrodes equally
D) Neither electrode
State the three products obtained from the electrolysis of brine.
practice_questions.marks: Hydrogen, chlorine, sodium hydroxide. [1 mark for all three correct]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at the cathode and anode when molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Cathode: aluminium ions gain electrons / aluminium metal is deposited [1 mark]; Anode: oxide ions lose electrons / oxygen gas is released [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why cryolite is mixed with aluminium oxide during the electrolysis process used to extract aluminium.
practice_questions.marks: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point [1 mark]; cryolite (a mineral) dissolves the aluminium oxide, which lowers the melting point of the mixture significantly [1 mark]; this means less energy is needed to keep the electrolyte molten, reducing costs [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student electrolyses copper(II) sulfate solution using inert (carbon) electrodes.

(a) State the product formed at the cathode. [1 mark]
(b) State the product formed at the anode. [1 mark]
(c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Copper (metal deposited) — copper is less reactive than hydrogen [1 mark]; (b) Oxygen — no halide ion present, so OH⁻ ions are discharged [1 mark]; (c) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — correct formula [1 mark], correctly balanced with electrons [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain the industrial importance of the electrolysis of brine, describing the products formed at each electrode and their uses. Include the half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and anode.

Higher Tier candidates should include the half-equations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three products correctly identified (hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode, sodium hydroxide remaining); explanation that sodium is too reactive to be deposited, so H⁺ ions are discharged at cathode instead; chloride ions preferentially discharged at anode over OH⁻ ions; industrial uses for all three products stated (e.g. chlorine for bleach and PVC; hydrogen for fuel; NaOH for soap and paper); correct half-equations written and balanced.
Secure: Three products identified with at least two uses; competition at electrodes explained; half-equations present but may have minor errors.
Developing: Two products correctly identified; some uses stated; half-equations attempted.
Emerging: One product identified; limited explanation of electrode processes.

knowledge_checks.q: What type of reaction occurs at the cathode during electrolysis?
Why is cryolite mixed with aluminium oxide in the extraction of aluminium?
options: To increase the melting point so the electrolyte stays liquid
To lower the melting point and reduce energy costs
To act as the anode material

knowledge_checks.q: During electrolysis of brine, _____ gas is produced at the cathode because sodium is too reactive to be deposited.
In electrolysis, the _____ electrode is positive and attracts negative ions.
Match each electrode to what happens there during electrolysis:

flashcard_questions.a: Using electricity to decompose an ionic compound into its elements.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the mnemonic PANIC used for in electrolysis?
At which electrode does reduction occur during electrolysis?
flashcard_questions.a: The cathode (negative electrode) — ions gain electrons.

flashcard_questions.q: At which electrode does oxidation occur during electrolysis?
flashcard_questions.a: The anode (positive electrode) — ions lose electrons.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three products of electrolysis of brine?
Why is hydrogen produced at the cathode during electrolysis of brine, not sodium?
flashcard_questions.a: Sodium is too reactive; H⁺ ions from water are discharged instead.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does aluminium extraction use electrolysis rather than reduction with carbon?
flashcard_questions.a: Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by carbon reduction.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is cryolite used in aluminium extraction?
flashcard_questions.a: To dissolve the aluminium oxide and lower its melting point, reducing energy costs.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the carbon anodes during aluminium extraction?
flashcard_questions.a: They burn away (react with oxygen produced) and need regular replacement.

flashcard_questions.q: What product forms at the anode when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed?
flashcard_questions.a: Oxygen — no halide ions present, so OH⁻ ions are discharged.

flashcard_questions.q: Higher: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode during aluminium extraction.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of using an electric current to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound must be molten or dissolved so that ions are free to move.
A substance that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water because its ions are free to move. Ionic compounds are electrolytes.
Solid electrical conductors placed in the electrolyte; the cathode (negative) attracts positive ions and the anode (positive) attracts negative ions.
An ion formed from a halogen atom (fluoride, chloride, bromide, iodide). In electrolysis of aqueous solutions, halide ions are preferentially discharged at the anode.
Concentrated sodium chloride solution (salt water), electrolysed industrially to produce hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
Al₂O₃, the ore from which aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.
A mineral (Na₃AlF₆) mixed with aluminium oxide to lower its melting point, reducing the energy cost of the electrolysis process.
The process of depositing a thin layer of metal onto an object using electrolysis, used to improve appearance, protect against corrosion or reduce costs.
